explain: An element: an opening tag, the content, and a closing tag with a /. Every piece of HTML is an element.
example:
po.wor:

Hi
remember: Open, fill, close: <tag> … </tag>. The / means "the end".

explain: Attributes go inside the opening tag as name="value". They add settings to the element; an element can have many.
example: po.wor: the links on the homepage.
remember: Attributes live in the opening tag only, never in the closing tag.

explain: Nesting: elements go inside other elements, like boxes in boxes. The page is a tree of elements. Close the inner one before the outer one.
example: po.wor: the planner list.
remember: Last opened, first closed (like stacking boxes).

explain: Void elements have no content, so they have no closing tag.
example: po.wor: the logo .
remember: Void = empty: nothing goes inside, so nothing to close.

explain: The page skeleton: head holds information about the page, body holds what you see.
example: po.wor: the top of every .html file.
remember: Head = thinking (invisible), body = what people see. Type ! then Tab in VS Code.

explain: Every new element you meet is the same shape: a tag name, some attributes, some content. Learn what the tag and attributes mean; the grammar never changes.
example: po.wor: buttons in the planner.
remember: New tag? Same shape. Only the names are new.
builtFrom: element + 3 attributes (one with no value) + content

explain: A form is just elements nested inside elements: a form, a label holding an input, a button.
example: The study app's Add syntax form.
remember: Big HTML = small elements nested.

explain: data-* attributes are normal attributes with a name you invent. JavaScript and CSS can read them.
example: po.wor: the speech bubbles.
remember: data- = "my own data" on an element.

explain: The frame every web page starts with. head holds information, body holds what you see.
example: The first thing you type in every new .html file.
remember: DOCTYPE first, then html → head (about the page) → body (what you see).

explain: Tags that name the parts of a page. They work like div, but say what each part is for.
example: A blog: header with the logo, main with the posts, footer with the copyright.

explain: div is a plain box for grouping things, usually so CSS can style the group.
example: Wrapping each product on a shop page in a card.

explain: Headings go from h1 (biggest) to h6 (smallest). p is a paragraph.
example: An article title, section titles, and the body text.

explain: A link. href is where it goes.
example: A menu that links to your other pages.

explain: Shows an image. alt describes it for screen readers, and shows if the image fails to load.
example: Product photos and profile pictures.
remember: alt = what you'd say if the picture didn't load.

explain: A form: a label, a box to type in, and a button.
example: A newsletter sign-up box.

explain: id names one unique element. class groups many. CSS and JavaScript use both to find elements.
example: Styling every .lead paragraph, and finding #intro from JavaScript.

explain: A bulleted list. Use ol instead of ul for a numbered list.
example: Navigation menus and feature lists.

explain: p is a paragraph. Browsers add space above and below it.
example: Any block of normal text on a page.

explain: strong makes text bold and important, em makes it italic and stressed.
example: Warning words like "Do not unplug".

explain: br breaks the line without starting a new paragraph.
example: Lines of an address or a poem.

explain: hr draws a line to separate two parts of the page.
example: Between two topics in an article.

explain: blockquote shows a quote from somewhere else, indented.
example: Quoting a person in a blog post.

Run npm start to begin.

line 1
  line 2 keeps its spaces
explain: code marks a bit of code inline. pre keeps spaces and line breaks exactly.
example: Showing commands in a tutorial.

explain: span wraps part of a line so CSS or JavaScript can target it. It does nothing by itself.
example: Coloring just the price in a sentence.

explain: h1 to h6 are headings, from biggest to smallest. Use one h1 per page.
example: Titles of the parts of an article.

explain: mark highlights text, small is for side notes and fine print.
example: Highlighting search results, legal notes.

syntax: <!-- This is a comment. The browser ignores it. -->
explain: A comment is a note for people reading the code. It does not show on the page.
example: Explaining a tricky part of the page.

explain: Entities write special characters: © & < > and a space that never breaks.
example:
Writing "

" on a page without it becoming a tag.

explain: ol is a numbered list. Each item is an li.
example: Steps of a recipe.

explain: A list can go inside an li to make a nested list.
example: Menus with sub-menus.

explain: dl is a list of terms (dt) and their descriptions (dd).
example: A glossary or FAQ.

syntax: Open in new tab
explain: target="_blank" opens a new tab. rel="noopener" keeps the new page from controlling yours.
example: Links to other websites.

explain: mailto: opens the email app, tel: opens the phone app.
example: Contact links on a portfolio.

explain: href="#id" jumps to the element with that id on the same page.
example: A table of contents.

explain: download saves the file instead of opening it.
example: Download buttons for PDFs.

explain: video plays a video. controls shows play, pause and volume.
example: A product demo clip.

explain: audio plays sound with play and pause controls.
example: A podcast episode.

explain: figure groups an image with its caption (figcaption).
example: Photos with a caption in an article.

explain: iframe shows another web page inside your page.
example: Embedding a map or a video.

syntax:
<svg width="100" height="100">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="tomato" />
</svg>
explain: svg draws shapes with code. They stay sharp at any size.
example: Icons and logos.

explain: picture lets the browser pick the best image format it supports.
example: Faster images for new browsers.

explain: table holds rows (tr). th is a heading cell, td is a normal cell.
example: A price list or a schedule.

explain: colspan makes a cell wider, rowspan makes it taller.
example: A total row at the bottom of a table.

explain: label names an input; for= must match the input's id. required means it can't be empty.
example: A sign-up form.

syntax:
<input type="password">
<input type="number" min="1" max="10">
<input type="date">
<input type="range" min="0" max="100">
<input type="file">
explain: The type changes what the input is: hidden text, numbers, a date picker, a slider, a file picker.
example: Settings pages and upload forms.

syntax:
<label><input type="checkbox" checked> Remember me</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="size" value="s"> Small</label>
<label><input type="radio" name="size" value="l"> Large</label>
explain: A checkbox is on or off. Radios with the same name let you pick only one.
example: Options in an order form.

explain: select is a dropdown. Each option is one choice; selected picks the default.
example: Choosing a country.

explain: textarea is a big box for many lines. A submit button sends the form.
example: A contact form.

explain: fieldset groups related inputs; legend is the group's title.
example: Separating shipping and billing details.

explain: datalist gives an input a list of suggestions while you type.
example: Autocomplete for a search box.

explain: nav holds the main links. main holds the page's main content (only one per page).
example: The menu at the top of a website.

explain: section is a part of the page, article is something that stands alone, aside is extra info on the side.
example: A blog: posts are articles, the sidebar is an aside.

explain: charset lets the page show any language. viewport makes it fit phone screens.
example: The first lines of every page's head.

syntax:
<title>My page</title>
<meta name="description" content="What this page is about">
<link rel="icon" href="logo.png">
explain: title shows on the browser tab, description shows in search results, icon is the tab's little picture.
example: Making a page look good in Google and in tabs.

explain: link loads a CSS file. script loads JavaScript; defer runs it after the page is built.
example: Connecting your CSS and JS files.
remember: link = CSS goes in the head. script defer = JS waits for the page.

explain: details hides content until you click its summary. No JavaScript needed.
example: FAQs and spoilers.

explain: dialog is a pop-up box. A form with method="dialog" closes it.
example: Confirm boxes and pop-up forms.

explain: data-* stores your own info for JavaScript. hidden hides the element.
example: Remembering which item a button belongs to.
remember: data- = your own notes on a tag for JS. hidden = there, but not shown.

explain: lang tells screen readers the language. aria-label names a button that has no words.
example: Making a site usable with a screen reader.
remember: aria-label = a name tag for buttons that only have an icon.

explain: style puts CSS right on one element. Fine for a quick test; use a CSS file for real work.
example: Quick experiments.

explain: The small picture in the browser tab (the favicon).
example: po.wor: every page shows the logo in its tab.
remember: Same <link> as the stylesheet, just rel="icon": the tab's icon.

syntax:
<svg viewBox="0 0 24 24" width="24" height="24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6">
  <path d="M4 7.5 L12 3 L20 7.5 L12 12 Z"/>
</svg>
explain: A drawing made of lines. In d: M moves the pen, L draws a line to a point, Z closes the shape. viewBox is the drawing's own 24×24 grid; stroke draws the outline in the text colour (currentColor), fill="none" keeps it hollow.
example: po.wor: the box icon in the header (its lid is one path).
remember: M = Move, L = Line, Z = Zip it closed. viewBox = the size of the paper you draw on.

explain: aria-hidden="true" hides it from screen readers; tabindex="-1" skips it when you press Tab. Use it for a decoration that repeats a link next to it.
example: po.wor homepage: the • and あ icons before the project names.
remember: aria-hidden = hidden from assistive tech. tabindex -1 = "minus one stop" on the Tab tour.

explain: aria-pressed says an on/off button is on. aria-expanded says the thing it opens is open. JavaScript switches them to "true"; CSS can style [aria-pressed="true"].
example: po.wor: the planner's "view" button; お手本を見る on the Japanese page.
remember: pressed = a light switch (on/off). expanded = a door (open/closed).

syntax:
Practice here
Examples here
explain: Tabs that screen readers understand. role says what each part is, aria-controls points at the panel's id, aria-selected marks the chosen tab. JavaScript shows one panel and hides the others.
example: po.wor: the 練習 / お手本 tabs on the Japanese page.
remember: list → tab → panel: a tablist holds tabs, each tab controls a tabpanel.

explain: title shows a small tooltip when you hold the mouse over the element.
example: po.wor: the planner's view button tells you its key is v.
remember: title = the name tag that pops up on hover.

explain: lang works on any tag, not only <html>. It marks one part as another language, so the right font and voice are used.
example: po.wor homepage: the あ icon is marked as Japanese.
remember: lang on <html> for the whole page, lang on a tag for just that part.

explain: Draws a line through text that is no longer true.
example: po.wor planner: ~~crossed~~ turns into <s>crossed</s>.
remember: s = strikethrough.

explain: rows sets the starting height in lines. spellcheck="false" turns off the red squiggles. placeholder is grey hint text that goes away when you type.
example: po.wor planner: the line you are typing on is a one-row textarea.
remember: placeholder = a place-holder: it keeps the spot until you type.

explain: <nav> holds a group of links to move around the site. aria-current="page" marks the link to the page you are on, for screen readers and for CSS.
example: po.wor: the icons in the footer of every page.
remember: nav = navigation. aria-current="page" = "you are here".

explain: A class on <body> lets one page get its own styles while sharing the same CSS file.
example: po.wor: the planner is plain white.
remember: Class on body = a name tag for the whole page.

explain: placeholder is grey hint text that goes away when you type. hidden keeps the input out of sight until JavaScript shows it.
example: po.wor: the Ctrl+M "move to a day" box in the planner.
remember: placeholder = a hint, not a value.
builtFrom: void element + attributes (one with no value)
